title: Noise-robust replay & priming cookbook for throughput benchmarking
content:
Purpose:
This is a practical, low-friction cookbook for running noise-robust throughput experiments against the serving runtime. It collects heuristics we've learned from flaky runs and aims to make steady-state throughput numbers repeatable without requiring heavy testbed changes. Use this for model onboarding, quantization impact checks, and perf regressions where noisy envs (scheduling jitter, cold microbursts, client throttling) distort results.

When to use this doc:
- You're seeing >5% run-to-run throughput variance with identical config.
- Comparing two model builds/quantizations and want a stable delta.
- Triage: is the variance due to client traffic pattern, serving runtime scheduling, or HW noise?

High-level approach (TL;DR):
1) Narrow the noise surface: deterministic seeds, pinned clients, isolated hosts.
2) Apply a two-stage priming: short micro-prime then ordered steady priming until occupancy stabilizes.
3) Run a multi-seed repeat suite with jitter-injection to catch brittleness.
4) Capture detailed telemetry (per-request timings, GPU occupancy, kernel timelines, KV hit-rate).

Definitions we use here:
- Primer: a focused set of requests used to fill KV caches, warm kernels, and align memory pools.
- Micro-prime: very short high qps ramp to wake up slow paths (30–90s).
- Steady primer: longer run to reach the target tail-latency and occupancy distribution (5–20 minutes depending on model).
- Occupancy: fraction of inference capacity (tokens/sec or active request slots) utilized; observable from runtime telemetry.

Typical experimental setup (minimal):
- Dedicated loadgen host(s) pinned to cores and colocated in same AZ/region as serving hosts.
- Loadgen binary with deterministic RNG seed, request trace file, and ability to control inter-arrival distribution (poisson, fixed-interval, jittered).
- Isolated GPU nodes (no other tenant workloads), or run on a reserved CI pool.
- Exporters enabled: metrics (Prometheus), tracing (Jaeger), GPU timeline (nvprof-like), and runtime event logs (KV ops, batch sizes).

Load generator config recommendations:
- Seed behavior: always set RNG seed explicitly. Default seeds cause subtle drift. Example flag: --seed=314159
- Sequence-length distribution: sample from production histograms or use three canonical profiles: short (<=64), mixed (avg 128, tail 512), long (avg 1024).
- Concurrency sweep matrix: run at target conc, target*0.5, target*1.5; focus on the plateau where throughput flattens.
- Arrival models: prefer jittered-fixed (fixed interval + gaussian jitter) over strict poisson for repeatability; add poisson-only runs as robustness checks.
- Request body variability: keep prompt text stable across comparisons; for tokenization effects, provide both real prompts and synthetic uniform-token prompts.
- Prefix caching tests: provide presence/absence primer sequences to validate KV cache warm-up behavior.

Warmup / priming protocol (recommended):
1) Clean start: restart runtime process(s) and clear runtime KV caches if possible. Note: on real infra this is disruptive; capture before/after if investigating cold-starts.
2) Micro-prime (60–90s): high QPS low-latency requests aimed to trigger kernel JIT/initial allocations. Use short sequences to maximize token rate.
   - Flags: --phase=micro-prime --duration=90 --seq-dist=short --concurrency=high
3) Drain step (30s): reduce to low QPS to allow background GC/async tasks to finish.
4) Steady primer (5–12min): run at target arrival pattern and concurrency with representative sequences. During this phase watch occupancy and GPU util trends. Only proceed once token-rate and 95th tail latency are stable across a 60s sliding window.
   - Stability threshold suggestion: <3% change in throughput and <5% shift in p95 over 1 minute.
5) Stabilization snapshot: record telemetry snapshots (metrics, kernel traces) at the end of primer.

Repeatability suite (multi-run):
- Per experiment do N=5 runs with the identical config and seed. For each run: full primer -> run for steady window (recommended 10 minutes) -> record.
- Compare median and interquartile TLS of throughput. If variance >3% investigate sources below.
- Run additional sensitivity checks with different seeds (2 extra seeds) to assert configuration robustness.

Jitter injection and robustness fuzzing:
- Intentionally add small request spacing variability (e.g., jitter sigma=10–20ms) to ensure the runtime's batching heuristics are not brittle.
- Add microbursts (shorted 1–5s bursts at 2–4x QPS) to test backpressure and queueing behavior.
- If the runtime uses client-side batching heuristics, exercise boundary cases (concurrency=1, bursty arrivals) to ensure fairness.

Telemetry to capture (minimum):
- request_rate (qps) and token_rate (tokens/sec) at 1s resolution
- per-request latency histogram (p50/p95/p99) and request-level metadata (batch size used, cache hit/miss)
- GPU metrics: utilization, memory used, SM occupancy, PCIe throughput
- Runtime internals: batch size distribution, queue lengths, KV cache hit-rate, kernel selection log
- OS noise counters: CPU steal, irq, scheduler migrations (for node-level noise correlation)
- Traces: end-to-end trace id propagated from loadgen through runtime to GPU dispatch (sampled)

Analysis checklist (quick):
- Do batch sizes align with expected kernel paths? Bimodal batch sizes are common when arrival discretization is off.
- Does median token_rate match expected theoretical throughput at observed average batch size? If not, look for memory or kernel stalls.
- Correlate GPU SM utilization dips with increases in queue length or p95 spikes.
- Check KV hit-rate: low hit-rate during steady state implies primer didn't match production prefix distribution.

Common pitfalls we've seen:
- Over-priming with only short tokens: primes kernels but under-fills KV caches leading to worse steady throughput for long sequences. Use mixed primers.
- Forgetting to pin loadgen threads: OS scheduler noise causes spiky inter-arrival times. Pin to dedicated cores.
- Using very long single-run durations without multiple seeds hides non-deterministic regressions.
- Comparing across different kernel builds without ensuring same deterministic launch flags (e.g., mixed-precision env vars) — always capture the full env dump.

Small runbook (step-by-step):
1) Reboot test nodes or restart services to get a clean baseline (if allowed). Note: restart adds reproducibility but can mask real-world warm state.
2) Start exporters and confirm metrics export.
3) Run micro-prime 90s.
4) Run steady primer 10 min or until stability criteria met.
5) Run N=5 measurement runs: each 10 min with same seed.
6) For each run collect end-of-run kernel trace + Prom snapshot + loadgen log.
7) Run diff script (scripts/compare-throughput.sh) to compute run deltas and annotate suspicious intervals.

Quick commands (examples):
- loadgen: ./loadgen --trace=traces/mix128.trace --concurrency=24 --seed=314159 --arrival=jittered --jitter-ms=10 --duration=600 --phase=steady
- clear cache (dev only): curl -X POST http://runtime-host:8080/debug/kv/clear
- collect GPU timeline: nvprof --profile-from-start off --log-file run1.nvprof ./launcher --args...

Notes & TODOs (non-blocking):
- Add small telemetry exporter to include 'batch_assembly_time' to catch client-side wait stalls (ENG-2097).
- Experiment with adaptive primer that increases primer duration for larger models ( >20B ) to reflect slower KV convergence.
- Write a short how-to for SRE on safe KV clears in prod-like infra.

References (internal threads & docs):
- loadgen PR with deterministic seeds: https://github.com/redwood-inference/loadgen/pull/412
- Slack: #serving-perf thread from 2025-12-08 (discussion about jittered arrivals)
- Related experiment notes: ENG-1189

Author notes (Avery):
This is intentionally practical and a bit informal — the priority is stable, repeatable numbers we can trust during model onboarding and perf regressions. If you copy/paste the primer sequence into an experiment, please add a short note with config used and any deviations.

End of doc.
